title: Dual-Head Knowledge Distillation: Enhancing Logits Utilization with an Auxiliary Head

problem.claim: Knowledge distillation aligns student predictions with ground-truth labels and teacher predictions, but converting logits to probabilities obscures indispensable information.

gap.claim: Combining logit-level and probability-level losses can degrade performance because of conflicting effects on the classification head.

contributions.claim: Dual-head knowledge distillation partitions the linear classifier into two classification heads assigned to different losses.
The method is motivated by an analysis attributing performance degeneration to classification-head collapse and contradictory gradients in the linear classifier.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors explicitly describe dual-head knowledge distillation as a novel method.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report that extensive experiments validate effective exploitation of information inside logits.
The authors report superior performance against state-of-the-art counterparts.

narrative_sequence.summary: Traditional knowledge distillation uses ground-truth and teacher probability predictions.
Probability conversion obscures information contained in logits.
Adding a logit-level loss to a probability-level loss causes performance degeneration.
The degeneration is attributed to classification-head collapse and conflicting classifier gradients.
Dual-head knowledge distillation separates the losses across heads, and experiments report improved performance.

source_observation.claim: Combining complementary loss functions can produce performance degeneration when their gradients conflict in a shared classifier.

interpretation.claim: Loss combination may require separating parameter roles rather than directly summing objectives.

application.claim: Consider assigning different objectives to separate prediction heads while retaining shared backbone learning.

exception.claim: The abstract does not establish whether this separation is beneficial beyond the reported distillation setting.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify datasets, baselines, metrics, or quantitative results.
The abstract does not detail the theoretical assumptions or proof.
The abstract does not establish reproducibility or independent verification.
